UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION




    Interconnection of Large Loads to the                                           Docket No. RM26-4-000
    Interstate Transmission System




         JOINT REPLY COMMENTS OF THE DISTRIBUTED CAPACITY PARTIES

                               CPOWER, SPARKFUND, AND VOLTUS



          The above-captioned Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“Large Load

Interconnection ANOPR”) has generated intense stakeholder interest; on or about November 21,

2025, 184 parties or coalitions submitted opening comments. The joint initial comments of

Cloverleaf     Infrastructure,     Spark     Community         Investment      Company        d/b/a    Sparkfund

(“Sparkfund”),1 and Voltus, Inc., (“Voltus”)2 highlighted the capabilities of demand-side and

advanced technologies to support the rapid interconnection of large loads, even when these

resources are located “off-site” or “outside the fence.” Similarly, the Joint Flexibility Parties

(Enerwise Global Technologies, LLC d/b/a CPower (“CPower”),3 Enel North America, Inc., and


1
  Sparkfund is a deployment services company that helps utilities take DERs from grid edge to grid core through its
Distributed Capacity Procurement (DCP) model, which enables utilities to plan, deploy, and dispatch DERs at the
scale and pace necessary to meet load growth demand and unlock the full value of the grid.
2
  Voltus is a leading distributed energy resource (“DER”) aggregator that provides a platform to enable consumers to
connect their distributed energy resources including demand response to energy markets. Voltus identifies
distributed energy resources, develops the aggregations, bids into wholesale markets, dispatches DERs, and
performs the settling and reporting. Voltus operates aggregations of DERs on behalf of consumers in every ISO/RTO
market in the United States.
3
  CPower is a national demand-side energy management provider that helps organizations use distributed energy
resources, including demand response, to support grid needs and unlock economic value. In this role, CPower

                                                   Page 1 of 8
 Voltus) suggested “that large loads . . . that enter into arrangements with another appropriately

located load aggregation to provide . . . curtailment be considered when exploring expedited

interconnection processes that respect existing queue positions.”4

         Given the breadth of stakeholder commentary and the accelerated timeline of this

proceeding, CPower, Sparkfund, and Voltus (hereinafter, the “Distributed Capacity Parties”) now

respectfully submit these brief reply comments to summarize and underscore the broad industry

support, as expressed in the initial comment round, for a comprehensive, technology-neutral

definition of large load flexibility to support expedited interconnection under ANOPR Principle

Seven.


 INDUSTRY AND THOUGHT LEADERS SUPPORT EXPEDITED INTERCONNECTION

                     FOR LOADS PAIRING WITH ADJACENT FLEXIBILITY

         As the Distributed Capacity Parties noted in initial comments, the ANOPR explicitly and

laudably recognizes the value of load flexibility and “hybrid” facility dispatchability in Principle

Seven, suggesting loads bringing these attributes should be prioritized for interconnection. The

Distributed Capacity Parties wrote that the new capacity need not be physically located at the

same facility, but “can be distributed across the geographic area within which the new load will

impact system constraints, provided that the system operator has the requisite level of control to

integrate the facility into operations and system planning.”5

         A variety of parties agree. In the context of new generation brought by specific large

loads, Exelon notes that “[s]uch resources may share a point of interconnection or be in close

(electrical) proximity to one another . . . and may warrant accelerated treatment to connect to the


aggregates flexible loads, offers these loads in utility programs and wholesale markets, and manages the dispatch,
performance, and settlement of these resources. CPower operates in ISO/RTO markets across the United States.
4
  Joint Comments of the Load Flexibility Parties at 4.
5
  Comments of Distributed Capacity Parties at 6-7.

                                                   Page 2 of 8
 grid” (emphasis added).6 Similarly, the Joint Consumer Advocates urge that large loads should

“offset their load through the addition of timely, local, and adequate capacity resources”

(emphasis added),7 supporting that capacity that is added locally, geographically consistent with

the constraints it is meant to ease, need not be within the fence line of the load site.

           Rewiring America writes,

           FERC should expand its expedited interconnection considerations beyond large
           load curtailability and co-located generation dispatchability to include
           appropriately located off-site distributed energy resources that can deliver
           curtailment or dispatch services under contract. These contracted resources should
           be evaluated as part of the interconnection package when they provide generation
           and/or transmission relief that offsets the impacts of the large load request. In this
           context, what matters is equivalent, verifiable performance in mitigating
           constraints within the same constrained transmission pocket or local grid area, not
           whether the asset is physically inside or outside the facility fence line.8

           Rewiring America expands the analysis to ANOPR Principle Three:

           [L]imiting combined studies only to physically co-located resources unnecessarily
           constrains the toolbox available to large load customers. Off-site distributed
           energy resources (“DERs”) can deliver the same types of energy
           services—generation, load reduction, or transmission relief—that on-site assets
           provide. Large loads should therefore be allowed to incorporate aggregated
           front-of-the-meter and behind-the-meter DERs into their interconnection
           applications to the extent those resources can offset the transmission or generation
           upgrades triggered by the request. For example, an aggregation of residential
           batteries capable of providing import or export services, or a portfolio of
           high-efficiency heat pump upgrades that deliver durable peak reductions, can
           effectively mitigate network loading associated with large load interconnections.
           A long-term commitment to secure and maintain such contributions should be
           treated comparably to co-located generation for modeling purposes.9

           Storage developer Eolian, an active participant and thought-leader in the recently

concluded Large Load Addition Critical Issue Fast Path process at PJM Interconnection LLC

(“PJM”), also supports the combined study of “load and proximate generation” (emphasis

 added), “including generation developed near publicly-announced load developments”

(emphasis added).10 Base Power, an expert in home backup systems, is more explicit:

         Base Power encourages the Commission to recognize that resource adequacy is
         not unilaterally bound by the physical location of the asset providing it. Resources
         capable of modulating their consumption or injection of power in response to
         system needs on demand, whether located at the load site or elsewhere on the
         system, offer functionally identical value to reliability and grid stability where
         modeled and verified in the course of typical, day-to-day grid operating
         conditions. The defining feature of resource adequacy is dispatchability, not
         geography. A resource that can increase or decrease its output or load in response
         to an operator signal provides the same system benefit whether it is co-located
         with the facility it serves or operates under a contractual arrangement elsewhere.
         Therefore, constraining generation in service of supporting new load
         interconnection dispatchability to a narrow class of assets would unnecessarily
         exclude a significant portion of capacity already supporting grid operation.11

         As these comments by innovative energy storage companies demonstrate, unlocking the

full potential capacity that can be provided by advanced technology developers requires

recognizing that appropriately located off-site resources provide network benefits on par with

those provided by on-site resources, and should be studied and interconnected with equivalent

priority.

         Emerald AI, a leading enabler of “on-site” flexibility of AI data center compute,

nonetheless includes adjacent or offsite flexibility in its four-category classification of data

center flexibility.12 Emerald AI notes the final category can “complement and augment the total

flexibility a facility can offer. Such adjacent flexibility refers to the ability to coordinate with

nearby or aggregated resources (e.g., a local VPP) via a software interface, so that the net effect

reduces withdrawals on constrained parts of the grid.”13

         Tesla highlights the value of distributed capacity, “urg[ing] the recognition of DERs and

VPPs as meaningful grid service tools that can support faster interconnection of large loads to the

transmission system. VPPs should be considered for their potential to alleviate transmission

network constraints and capacity needs associated with the interconnection of large loads.”14

DERs and VPPs are by definition not, at least in entirety, physically located on the site of new

large loads seeking interconnection; Tesla’s position emphasizes the need for the expansive and

comprehensive consideration of new off-site capacity whose network locations ease relevant grid

constraints, with the instant proceeding offering an unprecedented opportunity to “unlock a new

and massive category of untapped capacity to solve the growing pressure on the transmission

system.”15

        With respect to curtailment resources specifically, the Joint Flexibility Parties add

another dimension to the discussion, noting that “[n]ot all large loads will have the appetite to be

curtailable, but all large loads will almost certainly be interested in having access to an expedited

interconnection process. If another load or loads that are sited within the same stressed grid area

can provide the necessary flexibility, then the large load should be considered for an expedited

interconnection upon showing that it has entered into arrangements for such flexibility.”16

        The preceding excerpts highlight only a subset of the numerous stakeholder comments

that point to appropriately located off-site capacity as critical to the solution set and supportive of

expedited large load interconnection through contractual relationships. Advanced Energy

United (“AEU”) offers an appropriate summary of the general industry position on the value of

such adjacent flexibility:

          [Capacity] solutions need not originate at the site of a new large load but could be
         incremental flexibility that is contracted by that large load and that is located such
         that it counteracts the impacts of the new large load. That may require all or some
         of the flexibility to be at or near the site of the new large load, but some or all of it
         may be sufficiently proximate if it is within the same delivery zone or even
         wholesale market region. Because demand-side resources are not subject to a
         generation interconnection process, they can be contractually tied to the new large
         load while avoiding the undue discrimination concerns discussed with respect to
         Principle Three.17

         Recent research provides additional support for the value provided by adjacent and

nearby capacity resources to expedite large load interconnection. Enchanted Rock’s comments

reference a recent Duke Institute paper’s call for the clarification of “study timelines, queue

priority, and interconnection process for large load customers, as well as load-supply hybrid

facilities and pairings.”18 As the paper supports, such pairings can include contracted adjacent

supply: “[c]olocated or adjacent supply may be owned and operated by the large load customer

or contracted for with a third party.”19 Providing concrete quantitative evidence of the value of

nearby capacity, a detailed and fresh-off-the-press Google-sponsored research paper—published

yesterday and conducted by Camus, encoord, and Princeton ZERO Lab20—finds that data centers

can connect three to five years faster through a combination of solutions that includes off-site

accredited “bring-your-own-capacity” (“BYOC”).21 For a 500 MW data center, the study

 estimates 158 MW of off-site supply could be procured.22 Critically, the study finds that

distributed solutions significantly mitigate system costs borne by consumers, placing downward

pressure on rates in a load growth environment: “BYOC internalizes $326 million in capacity

costs per GW, with the data center procuring accredited resources directly and offering them into

the market to increase supply.”23


                                          CONCLUSION

            This ANOPR proceeding demonstrates broad industry and nationwide support to

accelerate the ability of our electric grid to integrate the large loads that will secure America’s AI

dominance. To enlist all available resources in this mission, the Distributed Capacity Parties ask

FERC to develop rules that allow off-site resources that are capable of addressing constraints to

be considered in joint interconnection studies and the expediting of large load interconnection

pursuant to ANOPR Principles Three, Five, and Seven. Such an outcome is consistent with the

emerging industry consensus, as detailed above.




                                                              Respectfully submitted,
